extracted.intended_audience: IP lawyers, in-house counsel, patent/trademark practitioners and businesses operating in Mexico
extracted.subtask_description: Country Q&A overview of Mexican intellectual property law covering legal requirements, exclusions, procedures, enforcement, remedies and terms for patents, utility models, trade marks, copyright, registered and unregistered designs, and trade secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable, an invention must: Be novel; Result from an inventive step (non-obvious); Be capable of industrial application (possessing utility). (Article 48, Federal Law for the Protection of Industrial Property.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories excluded from patent protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The following are excluded from patent protection: essentially biological processes for obtaining, reproducing and propagating plants and animals; biological and genetic material as found in nature; animal breeds; the human body and the living parts constituting the human body; plant varieties; theoretical or scientific principles; findings that consist in making public or disclosing something that already existed in nature; diagrams, plans, rules and methods for carrying out mental processes, playing games or doing business, and mathematical methods; computer programs; methods to present information; aesthetic creations and artistic or literary works; surgical and therapeutic treatment or diagnostic methods applicable to the human body and/or animals; juxtaposition of known inventions or mixtures of known products, or alteration of the use, form, dimensions or materials of such inventions or products, except when they are so combined or merged that they cannot function separately; or their particular features or functions have been so modified that they produce an industrial result or their use is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. (Article 49, Federal Law for the Protection of Industrial Property.)

rubrics_metrics.name: IMPI registers patents and can refuse grant on specified grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI) registers patents. The IMPI can refuse to grant a patent when the application does not meet the legal requirements for grant; the invention does not meet novelty, inventive step or utility; or the invention is against public order or violates a legal provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information on application procedure is available on IMPI website (www.impi.gob.mx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to patent applications — grounds and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A third party can oppose a patent application by submitting to the IMPI information showing failure to meet any of the substantive requirements of patentability (Articles 51 and 52).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions must be made to IMPI within two months of the publication date of the application in the Industrial Property Official Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for patent nullity/challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of a patent can be challenged through a nullity action before the IMPI on grounds including: subject matter excluded from patent protection; disclosure not clear and sufficient to enable the invention to be performed; claims exceed those originally disclosed; invention disclosed in a divisional application and includes illegal claims; patent has been subject to rectification or limitation; patent was granted in error or due to serious oversight, or was granted to a person not entitled; patent was granted in violation of the law in force at the time it was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidation actions can be brought at any time. IMPI can partially invalidate a patent and will explain changes in its final resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and start date
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent is granted for a period of 20 years from either: the filing date of the patent application in Mexico, or the international filing date in the case of a Patent Cooperation Treaty application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for patent infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement actions can be brought against parties that: engage in acts contrary to proper practice and custom in industry, commerce and services amounting to unfair competition related to patented subject matter; make unpatented products appear as patented; perform acts that confuse, mislead or deceive the public; manufacture or develop goods covered by a patent without the consent of the owner or appropriate licence; offer for sale or bring into circulation goods covered by a patent knowing they were made without consent or licence; use patented processes without proper authorisation (use includes manufacture, production, imitation, storage, distribution, import, export, offer for sale, marketing, transport and putting into circulation); offer for sale or put into circulation goods resulting from patented processes used without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and procedure for patent infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent infringement actions must first be brought before the IMPI. Appeals are to the Federal Administrative Court through a nullity claim or to the District Court by means of an Amparo appeal; the final appeal is heard by the Circuit Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fast-track or small-claims procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences to patent infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common defence is that the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be effective, a defence of invalidity must be brought as a counterclaim and submitted on filing the response to the infringement action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and preliminary measures in patent infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holders can request preliminary measures if they show ownership of the patent, imminent violation and possibility of irreparable damage; provide security or an economic guarantee; and provide necessary information to determine specific goods that are object of the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IMPI can order removal of infringing goods from circulation; forbid distribution or use; order seizure of infringing goods; order cease and desist; order suspension of services or closure of commercial establishment. Administrative infringements punishable with fines up to MXN21.72 million, additional fine up to MXN86,000 per day, temporary closure up to 90 days, or permanent closure. Once IMPI decision is enforceable, patent owner can bring claim for damages before the courts; courts will consider date of proven infringement and evidence of patent's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model protection conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: To be protected as a utility model, an invention must be new and capable of industrial application. (Article 58, Federal Law for the Industrial Property Protection.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and procedure for utility models
rubrics_metrics.description: The IMPI registers utility models and provides information on the application procedure on its website (www.impi.gob.mx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition procedure for utility models
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no opposition procedure against utility model applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model term
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility model protection lasts 15 years from the application filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model infringement, courts, defences and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement grounds, jurisdiction, defences and remedies for utility models follow the provisions for patents (see Questions 6–9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs that can constitute a trade mark
rubrics_metrics.description: The following signs can constitute a trade mark: denominations or visible signs sufficiently distinctive and capable of identifying goods or services from others of the same class or kind; three-dimensional forms; trade names and denominations or corporate names; the name of a natural person, provided it is not confusingly similar to a registered trade mark or a published trade name. (Article 171, Federal Law for Industrial Property Protection.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of trade mark registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is necessary as it confers the exclusive right to use a trade mark and to oppose third parties' use of that mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMPI registers trade marks and provides application guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The IMPI registers trade marks. Information on the application procedure is available on its website (www.impi.gob.mx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for refusal of trade mark registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds for refusal include: animated or changing denominations, figures or three-dimensional signs; generic terms; descriptive marks or indicative words; isolated letters, digits or colours; translation into other languages, spelling variation or artificial construction of unregistrable words; signs that include coats of arms or emblems of any political entity; geographically descriptive or misdescriptive marks; names of towns or places associated with manufacture of certain products; names, pseudonyms, signatures and portraits of persons without consent; titles of intellectual or artistic works, titles of periodical publications, advertising promotions and fictitious characters; trade marks that constitute false indications as to the nature, components or qualities of the goods or services; denominations, figures or three-dimensional forms identical or similar to a trade mark that IMPI considers well known or famous in Mexico; trade marks identical or confusingly similar to previously registered trade marks or trade names previously filed or published. (Article 173, Federal Law for the Industrial Property Protection.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to trade mark applications — timing and grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A third party can oppose a trade mark application before the IMPI within one month of the publication date of the application in the Industrial Property Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grounds to oppose are the same as the grounds for refusal of registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and timing for cancellation actions against a trade mark
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade mark registration can be challenged by cancellation on grounds including: non-use (if not used within three consecutive years before the cancellation action; action can be brought after three years from granting); registration granted in violation of the law (action at any time); prior use (if identical/confusingly similar to a mark used in Mexico or abroad before the application — action within three years of publication of registration); false data in the application (action within five years of publication); registration granted in error or owing to mistake/difference of judgement relating to a prior identical/confusingly similar mark (action within five years); bad faith (e.g., agent/representative registers mark abroad owner’s mark without consent) (action at any time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark term and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive trade mark rights start from registration. Registration is valid for ten years from the filing date and can be renewed indefinitely for further ten-year periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for trade mark infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement actions can be brought where a third party: uses a mark confusingly similar to a registered trade mark; without the owner's consent uses an identical or confusingly similar mark as part of a trade name or corporate name relating to products/services of the mark; uses a registered trade mark as a name, sign, symbol, initial or emblem; without written consent uses an identical or confusingly similar mark as a trade name/corporate name of a person whose activity is production, import or marketing of identical or similar products/services; uses a registered trade mark without consent or licence in relation to identical or similar products or services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and procedure for trade mark infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade mark infringement actions must first be brought before the IMPI. Appeals are to the Federal Administrative Court through a nullity claim or to the District Court by Amparo appeal; final appeal heard by the Circuit Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fast-track or small-claims procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences to trade mark infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common defence is that the trade mark is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be effective, a defence of invalidity must be brought as a counterclaim and submitted on filing the response to the infringement action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies in trade mark infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies are similar to those in patent infringement actions (see patent remedies entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of copyright protection — economic and moral rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protection gives the copyright owner moral and economic rights. Economic rights include exclusive rights to authorise others to reproduce the work; disseminate derivative works; distribute copies; perform publicly; display publicly; broadcast or communicate to the public through any means; import the work; use the work publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mexican law also provides for reservation rights granting exclusive use of titles of serial publications, names of TV and radio shows, artistic names, human and fictitious characters, original advertising formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright-eligible subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible subject matter includes literary works; musical works (with or without lyrics); dramatic works; choreographic works; pictorial and graphic works; sculptural and artistic works; cartoon and comic books; architectural works; films and audiovisual works; radio and television programmes; computer programs; photographic works; works of applied art; databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral rights protection under Mexican law
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral rights include the rights to disclose the work (disclosure right); be acknowledged as the author or remain anonymous or use a pseudonym (paternity right); prevent modifications of the work (integrity right); withdraw the work from the market; amend the work; object to the paternity of works created by other authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral rights are protected during the author's life and cannot be waived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal requirements to obtain copyright protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic requirements: fixation (incorporation of the work in a tangible medium of expression); authorship (only individuals can be granted authors' rights); originality of the work. (FLC.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright registration and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright can be registered with the Copyright Office. Registration is not compulsory and protection does not depend on registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, registration is necessary to enforce copyright as it is evidence of copyright ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright duration and related terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection starts from creation. An author's rights are protected throughout the life of the author plus 100 years after the author's death or the death of the last surviving author (for joint works). Droit de suite is protected for 100 years after author's death. Rights of actors and performers last 75 years from first performance, first fixation in a phonogram, or first broadcasting. Neighbouring rights protected for 50 years from first publication or fixation. Reservation rights last five years from issuance of certificate (one year for names of serial publications and TV/radio shows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for copyright infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement actions can be brought where: a licensee violates terms of a compulsory licence; a publisher, printer, producer, employer, broadcasting organisation or licensee concludes a contract transferring copyright in violation of the law; a published work does not include required mentions (e.g., 'All rights reserved') or the name of the author/translator/compiler/adapter/arranger; a work is published in a manner that damages reputation; the title of a work is used fraudulently causing confusion with a prior work. Certain acts for commercial purposes also qualify: using a protected work without prior authorisation; using the image of a person without permission; producing, manufacturing, stocking, distributing, transporting or marketing unlawful copies; commercialising a protected work without authorisation; using or exploiting a computer program without consent. (Articles 229, 231, FLC.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for copyright infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts that deal with copyright infringement actions include the Federal Court for Tax and Administrative Affairs and the Federal Circuit Court. The Copyright Office and the IMPI deal with administrative infringement actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fast-track or small-claims procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences to copyright infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common defence is to challenge the validity of the copyright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies in copyright infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunctions are the most common remedy. Administrative infringements are punished with fines ranging from MXN688,000 to MXN1.9 million depending on nature/severity, plus an additional fine equal to 500 times the minimum salary in Mexico City for each day the violation persists. Once the decision declaring the infringement is final, it is possible to claim damages before a Civil Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered design registrability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial designs that are new and susceptible of industrial application are registrable. A design is new if independently created and differs in significant degrees from known designs or combinations of known design features. Industrial designs and industrial models are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and procedure for registered designs
rubrics_metrics.description: The IMPI registers designs. Information on the application procedure is available on its website (www.impi.gob.mx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to registered design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no opposition procedure against design applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered design term and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered design protection lasts five years from the application filing date. Registration can be renewed for additional five-year periods up to a maximum of 25 years from the application filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for registered design infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: A design infringement action can be brought where: goods protected by an industrial design registration are manufactured or developed without the consent of its owner or without the appropriate licence; such goods are offered for sale or brought into circulation knowing they were made without consent; designs protected by registration are reproduced or imitated without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and procedure for registered design infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered design infringement actions must first be brought before the IMPI. Appeals are to the Federal Administrative Court through a nullity claim or to the District Court by Amparo appeal; the final appeal is heard by the Circuit Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fast-track or small-claims procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences to registered design infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common defence is to challenge the validity of the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies in registered design infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies for registered design infringements are similar to those in patent infringement actions (see patent remedies entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unregistered designs — lack of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no protection for unregistered designs in Mexico.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and conditions for trade secret protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade secret is any information of industrial or commercial application that a person keeps confidential to obtain or maintain a competitive or economic advantage over third parties, and with respect to which they have adopted sufficient means or systems to maintain confidentiality and restricted access. (Article 163, Federal Law for the Protection of Industrial Property.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secrets can be stored in documents, electronic files, optical discs, microfilms, films or any other known or unknown medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorised use of confidential information — civil liability and criminal offences
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual or company that hires a worker, professional, adviser or consultant to obtain industrial secrets will be responsible for payment of damages caused. The following are criminal offences: revealing to a third party a trade secret known through employment or licence; appropriating a trade secret without the right to do so; using information constituting a trade secret that is known through employment without consent of the person keeping it or its authorised user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for trade secret actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions for unauthorised use of confidential information may be dealt with by federal criminal courts, the Federal Circuit Court and civil courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fast-track or small-claims procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is not considered a trade secret and non-misappropriation defences
rubrics_metrics.description: The following will not be considered trade secrets: information in the public domain; information evident to a person skilled in the art on the basis of previously available information; information that must be disclosed by virtue of a legal provision or court order. The following will not be considered misappropriation: independent discovery or creation of the information; observation, study, disassembly or testing of a product or object available to the public or lawfully in possession of the person who obtains the information (provided no confidentiality obligation); acquisition of the information from another person legitimately without confidentiality obligation or without knowledge that the information was a trade secret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and criminal penalties for unauthorised use of confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common remedy is an injunction (preliminary and final). Criminal penalties include imprisonment between two and six years and a fine between MXN86,000 and MXN25.8 million.
